Neurology · published research

Acromegaly-related neuropathy

A single-case report recorded increased local foot blood flow during treatment. It did not establish recovery of sensation or daily function.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A single-case report recorded increased local foot blood flow during treatment. It did not establish recovery of sensation or daily function.

Summary of the Evidence

One human single-subject A-B-A case report was identified: a 48-year-old man with peripheral neuropathy following acromegaly and pituitary surgery. No independent replication, controlled cohort, animal model, or separate in-vitro study directly examining acromegaly-related neuropathy was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

The report used monochromatic infrared energy (MIRE) on the foot for five weeks, followed by a withdrawal period. Laser-Doppler measurements of red-cell velocity and concentration increased after the third treatment week, consistent with greater local microvascular flow during treatment. The patient had reduced plantar sensation and balance complaints at baseline, but the report does not establish a controlled improvement in sensation or daily function. An A-B-A pattern in one person can show that a measure changed during the intervention period, but it cannot establish how often that response occurs in other patients (Newton and Marshall 2021).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for neuropathy secondary to acromegaly was identified. Studies of diabetic or other neuropathies do not establish an effect in this endocrine-related condition.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or tissue experiment directly addressing acromegaly-related neuropathy was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The Anodyne Therapy System delivered 890-nm near-infrared light through foot pads for 15 sessions over five weeks. The report does not provide enough dosimetry to define a reproducible fluence or irradiance, and it contains no wavelength or dose comparison. This protocol is a single case and cannot set a standard treatment dose.

Interpretation

Local perfusion measures increased during treatment in the reported patient. That physiological change does not by itself show that sensation, pain, balance, or walking improved. The evidence remains a single-case observation, and controlled replication with patient-centered outcomes would be needed to assess clinical relevance.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for local foot-perfusion change in one case Very low for sensory recovery
Publications and records1 unique publication

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Laser-Doppler measures rose during treatment in one person, indicating increased foot microcirculation in that case. The report does not establish durable sensation or functional improvement, and there was no comparison group. A controlled study with sensory testing, symptoms, balance, and daily function would be needed to determine whether the perfusion change translates into meaningful recovery.
